utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djeric. The first matter we'd like to address is the attendance of Serbia and Montenegro in these proceedings. utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are aware but obviously we received the opposition, I believe, last night so we didn't have time to consider it fully. But we are able to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, well, that's partly due of course also to the late submission of your application. I would like to -- we are here to hear the 11 bis motion and not to spend the whole afternoon on this procedural issue. I'd like to give you five minutes to briefly respond to -- to the opposition by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe that here we are in the same position as in the Mejakic case. There as well we were not indicated -- indicated as a state to which a case should be referred by the Prosecution. Still we applied to have present in the proceedings on the basis of the principle that one of the accused there was our national. This is the same principle that we base our application on in the present case. We submit that two of the accused are our national. One is Mr. Todovic, and another is Mr. Jankovic. And I will further get later into the issue of the evidence for that, because that was also raised in the Prosecution's submission. Let me start with -- with the observation that there are several ways in which a state could appear in 11 bis proceedings in our view. First is if the state is being considered for a referral either because the Prosecution proposed that the case should be referred to that state or because the trial -- the Bench considers that this could be a possibility, and obviously the state should be heard in such a case. Now, another basis is that Rule 11 bis provides as we have repeated many times three bases for the referral or the establishing of the jurisdiction, territory or the place where the crime was committed and the state on whose territory the crime was committed, the state in which the accused was addressed, and secondly -- or, rather, thirdly, I'm sorry, it is the state that is willing and able to prosecute and has jurisdiction to prosecute, and this is obviously universality principle. Now, we think that considering Rule 11 bis under which a Chamber is in the position proprio motu to propose a state for referral in which the Chamber is in a position to consider any state it thinks fit for the referral in the proceedings, we think that on the basis of the fact that we are able and willing to prosecute and that we have the jurisdiction to do so that we could assist the Trial Chamber in making the decision that at the end of the day is just for the Chamber to which state the case should be referred. And these are the bases for our participation, our standing in the present proceedings that stem out of Rule 11 bis. There is another or third general basis, and perhaps this is the strongest one, and this is the fact that as the state of nationality of two of the accused in the present proceedings, we have an interest to have a -- we have such a strong interest to have a standing in the present proceedings and to ask that the case be referred to Serbia and Montenegro. Obviously this is a principle of parens patriae. This is the principle that the state of the nationality has the right to assert its interest in its own citizens, and this is a principle which has been a principle which has been a long standing principle of international customary law, perhaps one of the oldest, and under this principle we submit that we have standing under Rule 11 bis. Again, on the basis of this principle, we are in the position to assist the Chamber in making its decision, and at the same time we are in a position to protect our interests in our citizens. Now, I will conclude with one observation, and that is that from our practice with International Tribunal, especially considering Rule 54, different Chambers have been willing to allow or permit our state or other states to be present in the proceedings in which their interests might be affected. One of the examples would be several occasions in which the Trial Chamber in Milosevic case allowed Federal Republic of Yugoslavia then, and now Serbia and Montenegro, to be present. For instance, in a case where a witness was about to give his testimony, and we had an interest in this testimony, and at that time, if I remember correctly, Mr. Nice of the Prosecution was opposing this, and still the Chamber allowed us to be present to give our views, because the Chamber thought that, first, we have a legitimate interest and, second, that our submissions, our oral submissions, would assist the Chamber in making their decision. And I think this is -- the case is same here. I think that we have a very strong interest. I said it's based on international customary law. And secondly, I think that we are able to assist the Chamber in the present case.

Would I just like to make a small point on Yugoslav law on nationality. There are several grounds of course to acquire nationality, and one, perhaps one of the most frequent grounds for people from other republics of the former Yugoslavia to acquire Yugoslav or at that time Yugoslav nationality, at this time Serbian and Montenegrin nationality, was that they had residence in Serbia. At some point which was established before 27 April 1992, because at that time -- at that time, at that date, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was created.
