utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was established when?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: That was established all the way. That was established in 1977 Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia Criminal Code and continued until the present day. The provision in question was not changed. And I will try to provide you with the exact provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please perhaps slowly read that provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: This is Article 108 of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, paragraph 5 it says that: "With the consent of the federal public prosecutor," now it's a republican prosecutor of Serbia, "there could be in Yugoslavia prosecution in cases determined in Article 107, paragraph 2," I will come back to that, "if -- regardless of the law of the country in which the crime was committed if the crime that is going to be prosecuted at the time when it was committed could be regarded as the crime under the general principles recognised by international community." This is universal -- so everything that is recognised under internationality law as a crime can be tried with the concept of the public prosecutor and with reference to Article 107, paragraph 2 of the law, which says that -- which actually determines that -- that any foreigner who is present in the territory of -- of Yugoslavia can be tried for certain offences. But we can of course -- I know it's easier. We will provide the translation. But we had this also in the -- in the Vukovar case this morning, and I think that there is no dispute among our lawyers in Serbia that we have universal jurisdiction for international crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I do understand, under the condition that the person is present -- present on the territory of Serbia and Montenegro as it is now, yes. Which raises the following question: Mr. Todovic was not on Serbian and Montenegro territory when he was transferred to the Tribunal, because he was transferred from Republika Srpska. So if he would not have Serbian and Montenegrin nationality and if at the time of his transfer he was in Republika Srpska, you would then have no jurisdiction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. If he was -- if a person has not our national was not present our territory, obviously we would not have jurisdiction. At the moment the person sets his or her foot on our territory, we would have jurisdiction. And of course if the case is referred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: -- we would have jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Tribunal create you a jurisdiction by sending Mr. Todovic to Serbia and Montenegro. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Todovic is our national so we would not have this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Jankovic -- Mr. Rasevic, I'm sorry, that would be the case for Mr. Rasevic. But with regard to Mr. Rasevic, we don't actually push for our standing because it's much weaker than for persons -- for the accused who are our nationals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When Mr. Jankovic arrived at the Tribunal, he gave as his permanent address an address in Republika Srpska, not in Serbia and Montenegro. So I do apologise for making the mistake in respect of Mr. Todovic. But if Mr. Jankovic would not be a Serbian and Montenegrin national, then if he was present at -- on the territory of Republika Srpska, you would have no jurisdiction. He also was transferred from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entity of Republika Srpska, not from Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. If he were not a national we would not have jurisdiction unless there was a subjective element that he was present at our territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a couple of minutes to consider the issue at stake. Since -- yes. We'll withdraw for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter. The Chamber is considering that it has been shown the Mr. Todovic is at present a national of Serbia and Montenegro. We will proceed in respect of Mr. Todovic in a similar way as we've done in relation to the case of Mr. Mejakic. When it later will come to attaching weight to that nationality, then the -- it will be done in view of the history of how Mr. Todovic obtained that nationality. As far as Mr. Rasevic is concerned, he is not -- well, he's shown not to be a national of Serbia and Montenegro. As far as Mr. Jankovic is concerned, it's not shown that he is a national of Serbia and Montenegro, but, Mr. Lazarevic, if you would like to provide any further evidence on that matter, you may do so within the next seven days. This practically means that mainly on the basis of our finding in respect of Mr. Todovic that the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro may attend this hearing. We'll now move to the main subject of this hearing, which is the 11 bis application. Ms. Somers, if you'd like to make any further submissions, you may do so now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Because I do not know what may be raised in the course of the hearing, I would also indicate that whatever I say now, if I may have permission if need be to supplement it after other questions, as this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes it's very practical to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Particularly in light of hearing we have to have certain repeating issues, the concept of is this extradition or is it not, I would perhaps pre-empt the subject as it was done this morning repeat the arguments that were made that in fact the entire 11 bis proceeding is an execution of the mandate of the Security Council and that the right of the Tribunal in exercise of that authority given it to send a case that is properly before it to be heard in an appropriate jurisdiction as is provided for in 11 bis (A) is an absolute right, an unconditionable right, and has nothing to do with the concept of extradition. Again, it is a totally different animal. And to remind, although I'm sure the Chamber is very mindful, that in sharp contradiction to any concept of extradition, the Chamber keeps a very long but tangible leash on these cases by virtue of the provision in 11 bis, I leave it is (F), that is not something that is noted or would be part of any type of "extradition" proceeding. There is the ability to revoke under very specific circumstances. The role of the accused is, I submit, diminished in these proceedings. This is a forum issue, and basically if the Chamber turns its attention for a moment to the provisions of 11 bis (B), the decisional powers in the first instance to make requests lie with either the Chamber proprio motu, on its own motion, or the Prosecutor. The only mention of the accused for purposes of any input as to anything is an opportunity to be heard where applicable, where applicable. Secondly, if the Chamber turns its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doesn't that contemplate an accused who is not yet in custody and therefore not before the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Being in custody is not a requirement of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're not submitting, are you, that an accused has no interest in where he or she might be tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe the Chamber the Bench this morning used the term "expectations." There are expectations that the power to move the case around belongs to the Tribunal. I think that it is certainly in the interests where the Chamber believes or the Bench believes it appropriate to make an inquiry there may be certain factors but the power belongs to the Bench. And in -- even in terms, Your Honour, of revoking the language puts the request to the Prosecutor or the referral -- that the parties involved again are the Bench and the Prosecutor. And I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Somers, I just can't sit here and listen to that without responding. The party originating a motion is the Prosecutor or the Chamber may do it of its own motion. A proceeding having been originated, there is then I would have thought a very clear interest in an accused person as to the outcome of that motion, whether it be in accordance with the motion or a rejection of the motion or a decision on some other direction of referral. All of those things are alive, the motion having been moved or the Chamber having decided to take under consideration the possibility of referral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: An accused, Your Honour, who is before the Bench, certainly if it is deemed appropriate to or applicable, and that could be a circumstance where it is applicable. If there is something that the Chamber or the Bench needs to know, there may be very extenuating circumstances, but in principle it's a decision that is really made on the principle that the case is -- is possibly one that meets the criteria. Objections by the accused may not -- they may not be persuasive enough to change the course of a decision. But having heard it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nor the views of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct. We accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You seem to put -- what I'm concerned is the way you put it: It is as though only the Prosecutor and the Chamber that ought to be considering.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the principal moving parties are the Prosecution and the Bench, because we have an obligation to make sure that the case stays alive, and I think that the role of the accused is a minimal role in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think I've said enough to indicate I have, shall we say, reservations, and I don't want you to waste more time on it because you're under a short time pressure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd be happy, Your Honour. We have given written submissions on this, so I don't want to take up your time. The basis for our invoking 11 bis (A)(i) is founded on the territoriality principle as the first and I think the dominant one is in our view having heard what we've just heard, the only one that should be applicable. The crimes were committed and these are of course crimes that are deemed to be very serious crimes in -- on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We think that the record has been established quite well. Both cases -- both sets of accused have -- co-accused, whose cases have already gone through the appellate process. There is an extremely full record established by this Tribunal which should greatly assist the state court, and we're talking about a reference to the very able state court in Bosnia-Herzegovina to handle these proceedings. It should facilitate state the expeditiousness. It should also make it much more helpful with perhaps adjudicated facts. It is -- these are relatively small cases in the scheme of the cases of the Tribunal, and we think that all factors indicate that if the Chamber does grant referral or order referral, that of course the appropriate forum would be for all the reasons cited today and, in the submissions, Bosnia-Herzegovina's state court. If I may just reserve any further comment, I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Somers. I'd like to give an opportunity to Defence counsel to address the matter. May I ask you two questions before giving you that opportunity. You received the material in the Mejakic case so that you are aware of the exchange of views on those matters. Are you aware of what happened during this morning's hearing? Did you follow it? I see you're both nodding yes, which is now on the transcript. Could the parties agree that whatever has been said this morning in relation to the case against Mrksic and others that that would be part of the knowledge of the Referral Chamber in deciding the parties are aware of what has been said and can respond or react to that at this very moment, if they wish to do so. Therefore, there would be need to repeat everything. If the Defence would like to put its position, it could perhaps in this respect just briefly refer to, we take the same position as and then mention the subject matter relevant so that we know what your position is by consulting what others said. And if you would like to add anything or if you would like to make any reservation, please do so. Mr. Lazarevic, could I first give you the opportunity, and could I ask you to make clear when you speak for Mr. Todovic and Jankovic both and when you spoke only for one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. What I -- what my idea was is to first give arguments for Mr. Todovic, then after Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that Mr. Domazet could give reasons for Mr. Rasevic, and then at the end I would give some additional arguments regarding Mr. Jankovic in order not to mix up things and just avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Shall we first deal with Todovic, Rasevic, and then we'll hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can stipulate that we are aware of everything that this morning happened in this Trial Chamber. We were listening and following the proceedings in Vukovar group very carefully. Also, we received transcripts and the following documents in Mejakic case, and we are all aware of the content of all these documents. What we were informed is that we are allotted some 15 minutes per each of the accused to give our arguments, and we were asked not to repeat anything, and we will do our best to do so. For the benefit of the clients, I will now start speaking in Serbian, because they would understand that. [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Todovic within the time allocated to it will look at certain submissions made on the 28th of April. We wish to avoid any kind of repetition. First of all, the Defence will deal with the possibility of maintaining an international standard of a fair trial in relation to Mr. Todovic if the case were to be referred to the jurisdiction of Bosnia-Herzegovina for trial. The standards in the European Convention on Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, as well as the Statute of this Tribunal were dealt with in detail in our submissions, but the Defence wishes to give some additional views in relation to the right of the accused to presence and questioning of witnesses he might call for his defence if the case were to be transferred to the jurisdiction of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence of Mr. Todovic is not going to repeat all the legal provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure and all other relevant laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It will present its very own experience that it encountered when preparing the defence and the reactions of potential witnesses to the possibility of having the Todovic case transferred to the jurisdiction of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witnesses contacted by the Defence of Mr. Todovic expressed their readiness to come and testify before this Tribunal in The Hague about the circumstances they are aware of relating to the case, bearing in mind the fact that the Defence could familiarise them with all the rights that they can have as well as with the possibility of safe conduct for persons that may need this in the view of the Defence, and persons who may request that for their own protection. From my own experience I can say on the basis of my experience in the Bosanski Samac case, I very often requested that, and to my great satisfaction this was made possible, and in this way certain witnesses appeared who would not have appeared before any other court, but they did come to this Tribunal. All witnesses except for one who learned of this possibility that instead of testifying before The Hague Tribunal, they could give evidence before the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo withdrew their consent and expressed their fear that they may suffer certain consequences if they were to give such evidence. In order to be very specific, I will point out that practically in the case of Mr. Todovic these are three categories of witnesses. However, regardless of which one of these three categories of witnesses we look at, their reaction was identical when the possibility of having the trial held in Sarajevo was indicated to them. The first category of witnesses are witnesses of Serb ethnicity who live in the territory of Republika Srpska and who, during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were part of the military and police structures of the Army of Republika Srpska and other relevant organs. The main reason that these witnesses stated as the reason for their reluctance to appear before the court in Sarajevo was their fear that they themselves might be arrested and tried. They did not want to risk coming and giving evidence before that court. As Defence counsel, I could not guarantee their safety in any way from that point of view. Republika Srpska is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it said in its submissions in this case, and all the rights that the Prosecutor could resort to within Bosnia-Herzegovina are such that I cannot affect them in any way. However, the fact remains that such witnesses constitute a significant body of evidence that the Defence would wish to proffer. The second category of witnesses would be ethnic Bosniaks who live in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their main reason for not appearing before the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo was that people from their own community where they lived would stigmatise them as persons who were testifying against alleged war criminals and that they would be branded as traitors. Therefore, they were fearful for the safety of their own families if they were to testify for the defence of Mr. Todovic. It is a fact that before this Tribunal I have the experience of bringing such witnesses in, in other cases. They had no problem whatsoever testifying here before this Tribunal, because they felt safe because of the authority of the Tribunal, and also the protective measures that this Tribunal gave them were reassuring. The third category of witnesses that I had contact with and who changed their views with regard to testifying are witnesses who are citizens of Serbia and Montenegro and who, bearing in mine the fact that there is no institution of safe conduct in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they believe they would risk arrest and indictment if they were come and testify before the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bearing in mind what appeared in the Mejakic case, that is to say some 10.000 indictments of Bosnia-Herzegovina, perhaps these fears of theirs may be justified. For the most part, these are people who were in the army, who were in police organs and other organs, and who have good reason to fear for their safety and to be afraid of being arrested. At this point in time, I would just like to draw the attention of the Referral Chamber to the report on the state of the judiciary in Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 12th of March, 2005. That is a report of the organisation for Security And Cooperation In Europe. Mr. Todovic's Defence mentions this report several times in its brief and I believe it was also mentioned in the Mejakic case. I believe that this report gives me the right to say that I believe there are reasonable grounds for fear that it will virtually be impossible to have a proper defence for Mr. Todovic on account of the fact that witnesses simply will not appear. Mr. Todovic has a position of his own here, of course, and from that point of view he gave me instructions. He does not wish to bring anyone into that kind of situation, to be arrested or to be indicted because such a person would want to testify on behalf of his defence. Therefore, if the case is referred to the jurisdiction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he will not be presenting any kind of defence. On the other hand, as I already stated briefly, none of these problems would appear if the case were to remain before this Tribunal, and we would have no problem with bringing any witness to testify on behalf of the defence of Mr. Todovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, may I draw your attention to the fact that you are close to your 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. [In English] I apologise, Your Honour. It seems that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, many of the issues, many of the issues where you use -- where you explain matters which are in the substance the same that has been said this morning. So please proceed, but not for more than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the second question that the Todovic Defence wishes to elaborate on is related to certain personal circumstances of his. I would kindly ask now, if possible, to move into private session so that I could present these personal details of his. I promise that this will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there's no objection against the other accused being present and the representatives of the governments being present? Mr. Lazarevic? Yes. Okay. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, in closing, let me say that Mr. Todovic surrendered voluntarily. He put himself into the hands of this Tribunal, of the Court, with the expectations that he would be tried before this Tribunal pursuant to the Rules and Regulations and having full confidence in the equitability and justice shown by the International Tribunal and a lack of bias on the part of the Tribunal. I do not wish to say that he would not have surrendered, perhaps, had he had a clear idea that the Prosecutor would ask that his case be referred, but I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber or Referral Bench to bear in mind the circumstances in making a decision and that Mr. Todovic, when he made his decision, had in view the practice of this Tribunal, the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal, and the fairness of this Tribunal as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. We will have a break. After the break, Mr. Domazet, you will have an opportunity to submit further argument. After we're done with that, Mr. Lazarevic again on behalf of his other client, then the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina will have an opportunity to make further submissions. We will adjourn until five -- twenty-five minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to address the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I noticed that there was some disruption during a very short moment of the videolink. If there are major problems, I hope that there would be a possibility to address the Chamber so that we would be aware of it. Then we'll now continue. Mr. Domazet, it's up to you. You notice that I'm rather strict on time, but we have to be unfortunately. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try and adhere to the time limit and take up as little time as possible. First of all, thanks to the fact that these proceedings have -- these matters have already been addressed and I had the opportunity of looking at the transcripts of Mejakic and others, and I followed this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. morning's proceedings, I do not want to wish -- I do not wish to repeat anything that my colleagues already said, particularly not what was stated in the Rasevic Defence motion. But I should like to take advantage of this occasion to highlight a few points. First of all, some personal matters with respect to the accused Rasevic and those which have to do with certain dilemmas which the Defence has with respect to the Prosecution motion. Now, what refers to Rasevic personally is this: Since August 2003, he has been in the Scheveningen Detention Unit. He surrendered to the authorities in Serbia, and he was in detention there, and then transferred to the Detention Unit here. From October of that same year, I have been lead counsel on his Defence team, that is to say for more than a year and a half, and I'm saying that because that is one of the problems. Mr. Rasevic and I fear that we're going to encounter a problem along those lines if this case is referred to Bosnia and Herzegovina because our defence is nearing completion, and we were ready to go ahead, and we stressed at the conferences that were held, the Status Conferences, we said we stood trial-ready. However, unfortunately the trial did not come about, although in the meantime we had the co-accused Todovic here. So all the conditions were met, and I think that this Tribunal could have scheduled a trial date and that that would have been the fairest thing to do with respect to the accused Rasevic and with respect to the Defence team that has prepared itself for the trial and the Defence case. And as we were able to see from the submissions sent in from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the comments made by the individual Defence counsel that if the case is referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina that there would be certain changes, that it would have to be restructured or a new indictment written and a new pre-trial stage conducted. However, what Mr. Rasevic is personally concerned about is this: It is the question of time. He does not have anything against being tried in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if he cannot be tried here in The Hague, if he were to have a fair trial assured him there and if the trial were to be started within a reasonable amount of time and if it was completed within a reasonable amount of time. He's already been here for two years, and if he has to spend another two years before the trial goes ahead or is completed, then that would create a problem. It would be unfair towards him and unfair to the general proceedings. What he is particularly concerned about is his desire to have his Defence team that has been working for two years, he would like to have his Defence team continue working for him regardless of where the case is actually tried, and that would certainly be possible if the trial were to be referred to Belgrade. But that is not certain if the case were to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Sarajevo. I have seen assurances from Bosnia-Herzegovina that there is indeed the possibility, as opposed to Croatia where that possibility was excluded, the possibility of having lawyers specifically here from Serbia and Montenegro acting as Defence counsel in the trial. However, as far as I was able to see, there are no guarantees about that. It is a possibility that is open but no guarantees have actually been given. And what will happen if/when the case comes to trial Bosnia-Herzegovina does not allow for that possibility and does not allow Rasevic to have the Defence team that has invested such a great deal of time and effort in preparing his Defence case and also use the resources of this Tribunal? If the trial were to be held in Belgrade, that would not be a problem quite certainly. The reason that we mention Belgrade as a possible venue is precisely because of the fact that Serbia and Montenegro have done a great deal in recent years to establish a court of law. We have a separate prosecutor and Trial Chamber, and as far as I know, except for the Ovcara case, which is ongoing, is conducting another case that was referred to it and where the crimes were committed precisely on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am, therefore, quite certain that that Trial Chamber for war crimes in Belgrade would be able to take on the case straight away. I am not sure that the situation is the same in Sarajevo or, rather, if this trial were to be referred to Sarajevo, would it start straight away. That is not clear. All cases pursuant to Rule 11 bis which are referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina, would they be tried at all in Sarajevo or would they go before the cantonal courts throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina? And I am also concerned, and I will to repeat something that was already said today, the piece of information about 10.000 indictments are expected in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even if the number were fewer, this is a highly worrying figure for the effectiveness and efficiency of the courts and the proceedings held before them. So those, then, are the reasons for which the accused himself, Mr. Rasevic, was concerned, and that is why he wished his case to -- his trial to go ahead here in The Hague or to be referred to Serbia and Montenegro together with Todovic, who meets the criteria of citizenship which Mitar Rasevic at this point in time does not. However, he personally surrendered in Serbia and therefore meets the 11 bis criteria. The Defence is fully conscious of the fact that there are a number of other problems as well, problems with witnesses, for example. I don't want to repeat what has already been said, but just like what my colleague Mr. Lazarevic said a moment ago, those problems occur in this case too. We do fear that many witnesses, both ethnic Serbs and Bosniaks who have pledged to appear in court will refuse to do so and avoid coming in to testify if the case goes ahead in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that is something that is of great concern to us, because it can affect justice and fairness and the overall procedure as indeed the ruling that Rasevic expects, that is for the trial to go ahead as soon as possible. Let me also say a few words about the man himself. It is somebody who has spent his entire working life --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Despite the fact that you repeatedly told us that you're not going to repeat what has been said, and despite the fact that almost everything you said until now is already in the written submissions, we'd really -- this Chamber would like to hear additional argument, not mainly a repetition of what was said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no other separate arguments to put forward. I have told you of the arguments that were rightly used by my colleagues. I just wanted to say a few words about the man himself, and I was saying that he had spent his whole working life in an institution such as is a prison, the KP Dom. The war didn't bring him there. The war found him there. He was there when the war broke out. He stayed there throughout the war. He was mobilised, and also he worked there after the war. So he did not leave or escape anywhere or anything like that. He didn't flee. As commander of the guard shift, if that is command responsibility of any kind, if he perpetrated any acts, then it will be up to the court that's going to try him to say. But for all the reasons that we have put forward a moment ago which I had to repeat, I do agree that they have all been stated or most of them have already been stated before, but I have no others to put forward. That is what I wanted to say myself, and that is -- those are the concerns of Mr. Rasevic's Defence team, and that is why his main proposal was that this case should not be referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina but that it should be tried in The Hague. If that were not possible, then it should be referred to Serbia and Montenegro. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will really try my best to run only for 15 minutes. [Interpretation] Your Honours, in presenting additional arguments with respect to the request made by the Prosecution to have Mr. Jankovic's case referred to the jurisdiction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I should first of all like to say that we stand by our statements in our motion of the 6th of May. However, there is one matter that I would like to stress on focus on. The Defence never received a response from Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to the matter in hand and the Jankovic case. What I would like to clarify here and now is whether the motion was filed or not, whether the brief was filed or not. If I could continue, but perhaps this will affect further proceedings. I will continue, but if the registrar and the Prosecutor could let me know in due course later on of that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to me what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, these are two separate cases. I mean, what I received walls the answer of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Todovic case. The one that I have not received was the answer in Jankovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed it was filed late, Mr. Lazarevic, and it was filed something like yesterday. The Chamber has not seen it either. Perhaps this would be a moment just to put a question to the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina whether there's any reason for this late filing, what caused this matter, and if the -- whether the Jankovic response would, from its content, be different from the Todovic response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were problems. There were problems in correspondence. There is no essential difference between the two briefs in the Mejakic one yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it as far as the content, then, is concerned, that having read the Mejakic material and having read the Todovic response that that would provide an adequate basis for a response. Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm only asking that after I examined this response that I could be allotted some time. I don't ask you for anything else after that. Well, I don't want to make any delays in these proceedings whatsoever, just give me some time just briefly to answer whether it -- should there be anything different from Jankovic response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you make a reservation in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] The numerous documents and voluminous documentation that Bosnia-Herzegovina sent in and which contains a series of provisions within the scope of criminal law, legal proceedings, referral of cases, protection of witnesses, and other aspects represent legal frameworks for the application of law. However, in themselves, they do not represent guarantees of any kind, guarantees that the accused will be given a fair trial. It is the position of the Defence that regardless of how far a legal system is developed or not and how far a state is democratic or not, that there is no absolute ideal of a fair trial within a given system and that it must be assessed and evaluated according to each individual case before the courts. What the Defence would like to express as an anxiety, yes, I can say anxiety, is the complete lack of practice, practical experience on the part of the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. At this point in time, there is not a single judgement which could be the subject of an appraisal and assessment either by the Defence or by our colleagues from the Prosecution for that matter, or this Tribunal, on the basis of which we would be able to draw some conclusions as to whether the trial was a fair one and a just one, whether it was conducted according to the proper standards and whether the rights of the accused prevailed, were met. So that is our basic concern with respect to that court. Without a doubt, Bosnia-Herzegovina has made every effort in its legislation over the past two years, which was dealt with extensively. But for us to be able to conclude anything about the system and to say whether this accused or any other accused would enjoy a fair trial under that system, we're lacking practice, practice upon which to rely as a grounds. Therefore, I think that -- and although United Nations Resolutions exist that are binding upon the Prosecution in this Tribunal, I fear that it is too early to decide to refer cases to Sarajevo, to the courts or the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, until the court has had some practice and dealt with cases. The only way in which we can discuss the methods of which legislative system and the legislative system of Bosnia-Herzegovina functions is on the basis of reports by the OSCE, for example, to which we referred in our briefs and submissions. And I have to give you my assessment, without wishing to repeat myself, and it is that the legislative system of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not get a good mark from the OSCE. The judicial system didn't get a good mark. On the contrary, that many irregularities were noted in the functioning of the system, and that is all we know about the functioning of the judiciary system in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I should especially like to stress the position of the OSCE with a view to Bosnia-Herzegovina and that those reports cannot be said to be biased in any way. With respect to another fact in relation to Mr. Gojko Jankovic, I would like to express another anxiety on the part of the Defence team, and it has to do with the provisions of the law on the protection of witnesses that are under threat and are jeopardised. Without entering into the details, and this has been dealt with in detail in our brief, but bearing in mine the character of the indictment against Mr. Jankovic, we have every reason for serious concern in this case, if the case were to be referred to the state court in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the provisions would be strictly applied, that is to say the provisions of the law on the protection of witnesses under threat and jeopardised witnesses. That law was discussed in the Mejakic trial, and I'd like to indicate that in our brief we dealt with that extensively. But the fact is that if the Referral Bench or Trial Chamber were to grant protective measures to a certain number of witnesses, the Defence would be deprived of cross-examining those witnesses. The Defence would not be able to learn the names of those witnesses and that that would be in force for 30 years after judgement. And all that would be contrary to the standards of a fair trial as they have been established in the provisions that I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mentioned earlier on. We have already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're saying that anonymous witnesses are against a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do share, of course, the concern you express for anonymous witnesses, but would it not be helpful and would it the it not assist the Chamber to see what exactly where the limits are as they are established already by international courts on human rights because -- I'm not an expert in the field, but at least one could not say that the European Court on human rights would forbid at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's a general statement you gave rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, our concerned. I can elaborate if that is what Your Honour wants me to. [Interpretation] The Jankovic case is a rather special case before this court because his indictment included other co-accused, and there is already a judgement in that case, and even the appeal went through in the Kunarac case. As a Defence counsel who came across protective measures in this Tribunal, I believed that this victimological approach was quite correct and that it would be necessary in the interests of justice to provide a certain level of witness protection. However, measures granted before this Tribunal in the Kunarac case were quite sufficient to ensure the exercise of the right to a fair trial, because in these trials, it was possible for the Defence to cross-examine witnesses. They were made aware of the details of the witnesses on time, and they were in a position to prepare their cross-examination even including questions that had to do the credibility of the witness concerned. The provisions of the law that is in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that have to do with the protection of witnesses under threat and witnesses in danger, I want to quote this very specifically, I think they go a step further from the highest standards of protection that this Tribunal had, and that was the one step too many, thus affecting the right of the accused to a fair trial. That is our position with regard to these provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. [Interpretation] In conclusion, may I just say a few more things in relation to some of the concerns that the Defence has in the Jankovic case. Immediately after Mr. Jankovic's surrender and after he came to The Hague, Mr. Jankovic, via satellite, on television, watched the TV news at 7.00 in the evening, and the date would be around the 13th of March. In this particular news broadcast, different persons were giving comments on his surrender, presenting their own views on what kind of a criminal he was. Regrettably, we also have information these are some of the witnesses who had already appeared before this Tribunal. I have not seen this videotape, although I did take measures to get it. I'm just going to deal with this in one minute. After that, in a television programme entitled "Without Anaesthesia," journalist Emir Suljagic spoke to a certain Mr. Refik Hodzic. We have received information that Mr. Hodzic is one of the officials of the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to the information we received from the family, he was making inappropriate comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, either you provide us with this material or you do not speak about it. So therefore, it's of no use to tell us what you heard, that others told you what they saw on television without substantiating that by material. If you have it, fine; if not, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand your concerns and if you could give me just one second I will tell you what are the measures of concern to me, what were the measures that I undertook in order to secure these because that shows very much in detail what is the extent of cooperation of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina with counsels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you -- have you documented that? I mean, if you asked for their cooperation I take you've sent them letters?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes I'll be very brief. I've sent two letters asking for the copies of these two. I haven't received an answer so far. The letters were sent on 25th of April and 28th of April to Milan Trivic, general manager of Bosnian TV. I introduced myself, stating that I am counsel for Mr. Gojkovic. I asked for assistance and so far I haven't received the answer. This is what I wanted to raise before the Trial Chamber. And thank you, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lazarevic. I now turn to you, Mr. Halilagic. The Referral Chamber is aware that before we were informed about the wish of the government of Serbia and Montenegro to attend this hearing that you were inclined to just stick to what you had said in earlier cases. If there would be, however, anything you'd like to add to that, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall be very brief. As the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I wish to say that at this point in time, I do not see any need to file any other submissions in relation to what we have already submitted in writing and also at the hearing that was held in the Mejakic and Stankovic cases. We believe that the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina is in a position to take over these cases that are under discussion now in accordance with Rule 11 bis before The Hague Tribunal. Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the request of the Tribunal, on several occasions submitted information on relevant questions related to legal and practical issues. If necessary, we can give additional information regarding questions that have not been dealt with in our briefs. If you would like to hear our answers, could you please postpone that for another occasion. Bosnia-Herzegovina did not see any need to file any additional submissions. The Tribunal has been informed of this. However, in the meantime, the situation has changed. The delegation of Serbia and Montenegro appear, but we believe that it is inappropriate for the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the Government of Serbia and Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to be the only government present. We heard of this only last night, and therefore we were not in a position to organise our own trip to The Hague, but we heard about Serbia and Montenegro at such a late date. We are prepared, otherwise, to deal with any questions that you may have, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Halilagic. Ms. Somers, you asked whether could you brief and then supplement anything in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, you asked, since you were very brief, to be in a position to supplement, and we are at this moment hearing the parties and the government. Would you like to add anything in relation to what you have -- would you like to add anything to what you said in relation to what has been raised by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think Bosnia-Herzegovina very ably represented its position. The only thing I wanted to draw Your Honours' attention to is that the indictment itself contains a third individual. It's Jankovic -- Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Zelenovic, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that under Rule -- should the Chamber -- should the Bench invoke the power that is authorised under 11 bis (A), the entire -- if referral is ordered, the entire indictment then of course can be factored in and transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes of course there is the specific issue of the referral of a case of an accused who has -- who is still at large.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just to make things clear, this hearing is held for the purpose of hearing the parties, and since you cannot hear anyone who is still at large --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Understood I just wanted to because of the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might deal with that in written submissions rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The other point is that the issue of accused Rasevic, perhaps being -- because of the -- well, the content of the nationals -- well, splitting the case would be inappropriate. The idea is to keep all accused together. So if the referral of course is made, then we of course advocate that all should -- the entire transfer should include the -- the whole group of accused. Thank you very much, Your Honours, for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, having heard the parties and having heard the government of the state specifically mentioned in the request by the Prosecution, I now turn to the representative of -- representatives of Serbia and Montenegro. In other cases you have expounded on developments in your law. You have expounded on -- I would say on how Serbia and Montenegro could cope with a referral. The Chamber is aware of that. I take it that the main reason for your present -- presence at this moment is to perhaps add some specific reason apart from the general reasons you've given already this morning in other cases such as whether a trial preferably should be held close to the victims or, rather, to the place where some other evidence is. So therefore, if there's any very specific reason why in respect of your national this case should preferably be heard in Belgrade rather than in Sarajevo, you have an opportunity to briefly address that specific matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The main purpose, of course, of our submissions in this case is to state our ability -- to state that we are able and willing to take up the case and that we are adequately prepared to do so, to accept the case. Therefore, in light of our arguments made this morning to which we stick in this case as well, I would just say that on the basis of Rule 11 bis (A), we think that we fall under the jurisdictions that may be considered for referral, and we do not have to add anything specific. We would just like to reiterate our argument that the Chamber should primarily look into the issue of the fairness of the trial and compare possibilities in that respect, and we are confident, of course, that the Chamber will do so. Therefore, we don't have anything specific to add to our morning submissions. There is just one small point, and this is related to the submission of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this case as well as in Mejakic case, which provide us with an interpretation of -- of the implementation of the doctrine of superior responsibility in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course we are not contesting this interpretation. It's a reasonable interpretation. But we have some reservations in the same way as for instance amicus curiae in Norac Professors Damaska and Krapac had some reservations. In other words, we think that it is more appropriate to try to interpret the law applicable -- the criminal law applicable to the case to produce the same effects as the -- same effects as possible as the doctrine of superior responsibility, but we have certain -- some reservations as to the applicability of international customary law, direct applicability of international customary law of superior responsibility. However, I repeat we are not contesting the argument. We are just -- proposed by Bosnia and by the Prosecution, we are just -- we just think that it would be more appropriate to give weight to the opinion of amicus curiae. And with this I conclude my observations and just would like to repeat that we stand by our submissions in our written submission of the 6th of May this year. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So just to briefly summarise, there are no very specific reason for these -- from this case apart from one of the accused is one of your nationals and you have set out before the importance of -- the importance of and the advantages of trying those cases in Belgrade rather than at any other place. Since your position directly affects the position of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would like to give you, Mr. Halilagic, an opportunity to respond. It was appreciated that the representative of Serbia and Montenegro did not start a battle, a kind of a beauty contest on who is the best but just explained his -- what the availability of the -- of the judicial structure in Serbia and Montenegro to try this case. Would you like to respond? Or would you like to make any further submissions, because it's not a debate between you and Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Again I'm going to be brief. On behalf of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I wish to guarantee all the accused a fair trial. I have been working for the Ombudsman for already eight years, and we know that the relevant convention is being applied. We can guarantee a fair trial with giving guarantees to all the accused that they can present their defence properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were your submissions. Then we'll have an opportunity now to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber suggests that we have a short break, that we'll use that break also to see whether we have any additional questions. Then the parties will have a brief opportunity to make any final observations they'd like to make. We have a break until twenty-five minutes to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to put a few questions. Mr. Lazarevic, you have written submissions. You stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina has not ratified the European Convention on mutual Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assistance in criminal matters. Are you aware that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand what Your Honour is referring at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware that Bosnia-Herzegovina meanwhile did?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not aware of that situation, and I am grateful to Your Honour for sharing this information with me in this case. I withdraw this part of my motion and ask for it to be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out. Would that have, in your view, consequences for the safe conduct issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact I believe it would have. Also, I cannot be completely certain unless I look at this ratification, whether there are any reserves on this ratification, whatever. I mean, I am not aware of this, I am not expert in constitutional law should any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but basically it would certainly make some difference. And while I do believe that it will assist the Defence in many ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also perhaps it might have some consequences in terms of forcing witnesses residing abroad to testify, because I think you rightly indicated that -- and you gave us an example if the case would be heard in Bosnia and Herzegovina that there would be no way to force witnesses to appear from Serbia and Montenegro, but of course the same would be true the other way around, that under this convention there always would be a possibility of letters rogatory in which the witness could be heard if need be under oath in his own territory. So that would be on both sides. And I take it, but I'm now addressing both the Serbia and Montenegro and the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina that if the case would be referred and to whatever state it would be referred that the state to which it would not be referred would assist by positively responding on requests for letters rogatory. Is that a correct understanding? I first address you, Mr. Halilagic. Is my assumption correct that if the case would be referred to Serbia and Montenegro that Bosnia and Herzegovina, under its treaty obligations, European Convention on Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters would assist for example by executing letters rogatory?

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, we would take all the necessary steps for our part. And if I might be able to state a sentence with respect to the convention, may I go ahead with respect to the convention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We ratified the convex, but I wish to stress that we applied the convention regardless of the fact that it wasn't ratified. So even before it wasn't ratified. So even before its ratification we applied it. I work in the ministry of justice, and I know that in all cases we did apply the convention fully regardless of the fact that it wasn't ratified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that we will fully apply the provisions of the convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for that answer. Mr. Lazarevic, in the written submissions, in paragraph 72, the last one, you more or less stated that if an accused would have access to testimony in other cases which might become evidence, only -- would have access to it only by listening to tapes, then that would be a violation of a basic right of the accused, and then you specifically mentioned to be informed promptly on the nature and the course of the accusation. My question is: Access to potential evidence, isn't that something different from being informed promptly on the nature and the course of the accusation, because you put the two together as if it were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to Your Honour, and perhaps I was misunderstood. The access to the -- to the evidence is one issue, and Your Honour is quite right, is another issue, but in our view it was related to each other, because after reading -- after reading the proverbs of Bosnian code of criminal proceedings, it seems that the Prosecution -- that the prosecutor's office in Bosnia-Herzegovina is not limited with -- with the indictments of this Tribunal, and they have the right to exceed the limits of these. They have the right to amend the indictment with some other accused, with some additional factual allegations. So in a way that if such a situation happens, this is the way we see the connections between the access to the -- to the evidences and the right of the accused to be fully informed of what the charges are. So that's the sense in which we explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It sounds as if you're introducing even a third element, and that is a kind of rule of speciality that one should only be prosecuted for the crimes for which you have been referred. That's -- and not for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not stating there is any rule with imposition of -- I understand that. That is not what I'm stating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question for the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you inform the Chamber about any regulations concerning remuneration of Defence counsel before the state court, and I am referring to assigned Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina have brought in provisions concerning remuneration for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from provisions, is there a budget as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Finally, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any specific regulation on, well, let's say the remuneration as such, so not to the right to have counsel assigned, because that is among the material that you have sent, but if there are any specific regulations and if there are any specific measures taken in respect to the budget, the Chamber would like to receive a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. You will receive a copy with respect to remuneration for Defence counsel. A copy of the decision of ministers, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So information as complete as possible. If there would be any measure taken in terms of budget, then this would certainly assist the Chamber when it -- when it seeks, whether it can be satisfied that the fair trial is guaranteed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like -- once again like to stress that we in Bosnia-Herzegovina apply the most modern world standards fully. The European Convention is a component part of the human rights convention and Bosnia-Herzegovina gives full guarantees and its law does that the standards will be respected fully. In addition to that, Bosnia-Herzegovina has prepared all other necessary measures to enable a fair trial for all accused in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halilagic. I finally have the following question. Whoever can answer it may do so. Many references were made today to OSCE reports on the practice in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. These reports were not always without critical notes on these practices. Do there exist similar reports in respect of the practice in Serbia and Montenegro? Just to explain to you what my problem would be, there do not exist any reports on my ability to play tennis. However, there are some reports that the tennis of my neighbour is not as good as it could be. Nevertheless, my tennis is worse than that of my neighbour. I hope you understand what the issue is. Whoever wants to answer the question may do so. Yes, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I -- we have a mission of the OSCE in Serbia and Montenegro. I believe they have a regular -- regular reports on various aspects of -- on various matters that are in their mandate in the same way as in Croatia. I cannot refer you to specific reports. They can be supplied, and I think it's available on the Internet. I think that the last report was sometime around 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that specifically on the prosecution of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I cannot confirm that. What I can say is that I have seen a Human Rights Watch report, maybe you're aware of it, that covered all the states on the territory of former Yugoslavia, or at least Bosnia, Croatia, and Serbia and Montenegro, and this is also some -- some information on this -- on this issue. But I cannot -- we can do a research and then file later. I'm not aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In you say it is on the Internet and if the parties would agree that whatever Human Rights Watch reports and OSCE reports are published on the Internet, so public documents, could be consulted by the Chamber, then we certainly would be able to find them. These are, then, more or less legal sources rather than matters that are in need of evidence here at this moment. I see Prosecution nodding yes. Defence would also agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for this assistance. Any further answers to that question? Then I have no further questions. The Bench has no further questions. I'd like to give an opportunity to both parties to make any final observations. Ms. Somers you're not obliged to do it, if you say everything has been said that should be said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This has been a very long day for all parties and I'm trying not to repeat. The Prosecution in the earlier cases that were heard in March of this year when Serbia and Montenegro were invited, albeit they were not part of the initial referral, in no way by participating in such a hearing in no way that would serve as a waiver of what we have interpreted as the rules requirement of who can make the request, and we're clearly standing, Your Honours, by our recent submissions. We understand what the Chamber's ruling was, but we think that it can become perhaps complicated ultimately if this type of last-minute event were a pattern and we have a concern for that. If in fact these cases are referred, we of course believe that the appropriate and sole venue should be Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think it's amplified today by comments about the changes. Bosnia has indicated it's been mindful of some of the comments that were made at earlier hearings about are they becoming party to certain conventions, and they in fact have continued to make the efforts that were required to bring them into compliance with the concerns that were raised by this Chamber about things such as safe conduct, witness protection, et cetera. The referral to Bosnia-Herzegovina, if referral is granted fits squarely within the rule and fairly within the rule without any type of manoeuvering, and we hope that if there are any further questions that may arise at any point, I believe the Chamber -- the Bench had offered some extended time period. It seems some mention of some seven days for some submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven days, that was only for the nationality of one of the accused. That's not the substance. It's mainly the procedural issue that was at sake.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If anything came up that required comment we would seek permission to do so. Thank you very much for the audience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Defence. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Bearing in mind that I briefly have to sum up what my client drew as his own conclusion and bearing in mind the instructions he gave me, I just wish to say the following: Mr. Todovic, from 1997 when his indictment was made public, left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina under threat. Immediately afterwards, his family did too. After that, the Krnojelac trial took place and these threats continued both vis-a-vis himself and the members of his family. Finally, when he surrendered, the threats intensified even intensified even further and that's why the question of his safety was raised by his attorney. Mr. Todovic, bearing in mind the fact that he spent his entire life and career in judicial authorities and also in correctional facilities, it is not possible to provide them with a fair trial, him personally, before any court of law in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, he believes that it would be fair to him that if this trial does not wish to -- if this Tribunal does not wish to deal with this trial that he be sent to a third country. If he were to be referred to any other country and in this respect he primarily means Serbia and Montenegro who have expressed the wish, he will certainly not appeal any such ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very brief. I will basically just repeat what I said at the very end. My client, Mitar Rasevic, wishes for his trial to start as soon as possible whether that is going to be in The Hague or Sarajevo or Belgrade is for you to decide. He trusts your decision and he just wants to have fair conditions ensured to him, a proper defence, and he wants the trial to take place as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Lazarevic, for your second client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As for Mr. Gojko Jankovic, I have to say that regardless of the assurances we received from the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who themselves guaranteed a fair trial just now, I'm afraid that this is a guarantee that is not sufficient, especially not in relation to Mr. Jankovic bearing in mind the nature of the accusations levelled against him and the facts that are already mentioned to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Court, and unfortunately because of the lack of cooperation on the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina I could not have presented this evidence to the Court. I promise if there is anyway for me to do so that I shall present you with this evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from some documents in the public domain, legal texts, press releases, et cetera, the Chamber received three letters about the nationality of the three accused, the letters dated the 4th of April, 2005. Since much has been said about the letters and nationality, we'd like to mark them for identification so that it's clear. Mr. Usher, could you -- Mr. Registrar, would you please assign numbers to these three letters concerning each accused so that they're marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you wish a formal motion for -- to have them moved into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to tender them into evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution does request that these items be marked and tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence? Is there any? No. I note that these are just the informal translations of those letters and not the originals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sir, the -- I will submit them. They were on Sanction. The B/C/S version is on Sanction, and that was the translation that was provided. But we will resubmit them with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be acceptable for the Defence if there. Would be any -- any problem of course the Defence could address the Chamber. I take it that no response is a response that there's no objection. Well, then, if you assign numbers to the -- and already take into account that the originals will receive a number as well. Since the cases have the same numbers as the normal cases, we will assign "R" numbers, which are referral numbers. So not specifically Prosecution but they are tendered by the Prosecution, are admitted as R1, 2, and 3. Mr. Registrar, number 1 would be the letter concerning Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Number R1 will concern the letter regarding Mr. Mitar Rasevic. R2 will be the letter concerning Mr. Savo Todovic. As to the third letter, R3 will concern Mr. Gojko Jankovic, bearing in mind that the three letters were -- are in English and the original in B/C/S which will be communicated later on to the Registry. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This concludes the hearing. I address the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Halilagic, you indicated to the legal officer of the Referral Chamber that you might need to ask for a further delay since you were a bit surprised by the developments in view of the presence of the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro. May I take it that there's no need or would you ask for any further delay?

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I give up on that request. We have said everything we have to say. I hope that we will proceed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It's only a technical issue probably, but having in mind that these three letters have been tendered into evidence and then one of them deals with Mr. Todovic's nationality and citizenship, saying probably that he's not a citizen of Serbia and Montenegro, and that we have other document challenging this letter, should I be allowed to tender this also into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is a copy available, that would then get number R4. Is this the Prosecution aware of the contents of the document? Has it seen it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have seen nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have seen nothing. Would you have a spare copy? Could it first be shown to the -- is there any translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The only one that we have in B/C/S. It's a formal decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll be allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you will allowed to provide this within the same seven days. You can add that to the material in respect of the nationality of -- of this accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to this discussion, would the Chamber consider requesting of the Defence the application, a copy of the application for citizenship? It perhaps might also lend some insight into the sequence of events that seem to be somewhat at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it -- does there exist a copy of the application?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't have a copy of it. Since it was done through the embassy, I do believe that there is a record on this, and I believe that representatives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we take the same rule that if you think it's of any assistance for your, I would say, claim of nationality for whomever of the three accused you may do so, but within the next seven days. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: We are at the disposal of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: -- and we can supply ourselves the necessary document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'd rather have it done by the Defence counsel, then. And if there's nothing else, I would like to thank the -- the original in B/C/S already provided receives number R4, and we expect a translation to be provided. To that extent, it's provisionally admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This, then, concludes the 11 bis hearing. I'd like to thank the representatives of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro. We stand adjourned, and a decision will be given in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 6.07 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Rule 11 bis hearing adjourned
